subtype: Approach: rehearsing aloud with a timer [Action]
passage: The final review was at ten the next morning, and Pradeep sat in the flat with a stopwatch, a bottle of water and the printed slides. First run: fourteen minutes. Jahnavi came over after dinner and listened to the third run from the sofa, and said the middle was where her attention drifted. Pradeep cut two sentences and one chart. The last run ended at nine minutes fifty seconds. Pradeep wrote the time on a sticky note and stuck it to the laptop lid, glad to know exactly how long the talk would last.

subtype: Approach: rehearsing aloud with a timer [Action]
passage:
'Ready? Timer's on,' Reena said, holding up her phone. 'Ten minutes. Go.'
Hrithik stood in the hostel common room, facing her and a row of empty chairs. 'Good morning. Our project looked at why tomato prices swing so wildly in our district...'
He went through the problem, then the method: the survey of forty farmers, the market data, the three cold-storage sites. At the results slide Reena raised the phone. 'Eight minutes gone.'
'What? I've still got results and recommendations.'
'You spent almost five minutes on the method. The part about the storage sites went on and on.'
Hrithik sat down on a chair. 'That's my second run today. The first one was long too. I just didn't time it.'
'So cut the storage sites to one slide. Say the number, move on.'
He crossed out two slides and stood up again. Third run: 9 minutes 40 seconds. Reena clapped.

qa.q: How many farmers were in the survey?
How did Hrithik feel when Reena said eight minutes were gone?
qa.a: He was shocked and a bit deflated, realising the method section had eaten most of the time.

qa.q: What else could Hrithik do before the real talk?
qa.a: Run it once more with the timer and set a checkpoint, such as being at the results by minute five.

qa.q: What is the rehearsal like for Reena?
qa.a: Reena acts as timekeeper and honest listener, spotting the long middle and cheering when the talk fits.

grounding: Shows a student rehearsing aloud with a timer and a friend, finding the middle section runs long and cutting it to fit ten minutes.

subtype: Approach: rehearsing aloud with a timer [Action]
passage:
I'm Tanuja, and before my first big class presentation I thought rehearsal meant reading my slides in my head. My sister made me do it properly.
The first run, alone in my room, out loud, with the phone timer: fourteen minutes. The limit was ten. I had no idea where the time went.
The second run I timed each part. Introduction: one minute. Background: two. The middle part, where I explained my survey method, took seven minutes. Seven! I'd been explaining every single question in the questionnaire.
I cut the method to three questions as examples and one sentence about the rest. The third run I did for my classmate Imran in an empty classroom after lunch. Ten minutes and twenty seconds. He said the middle still dragged a little, so I cut one more example.
On the day, I finished at 9:50. I've never felt so calm at the front of a room.

qa.q: How long did the middle part take in the second run?
How did Tanuja feel on the day, finishing at 9:50?
qa.a: Tanuja felt calm and in control, which had never happened before at the front of a room.

qa.q: What else could Tanuja add to the rehearsal next time?
qa.a: Practise answering a question or two after the timed run, since questions also take time.

qa.q: How might Imran have felt watching the third run?
qa.a: Imran was probably glad to help and honest enough to say the middle still dragged.

grounding: Shows a student rehearsing a talk three times aloud with a timer, once for a friend, and trimming a long middle section to fit ten minutes.
